description: A cairn that got up. Moss on every weathered face, a flat head low in the shoulders, one fist that opens ground.
lore: Count the dead who ever cleared stones off a field before they could work it, and you have counted a good share of everybody. Every one of those fields had a heap at the edge of it — near enough the same heap in every country and every century: rounded brown stones, waist-high, added to a little each season. Seen daily by whoever worked the ground. Walked around, never walked on, put to no further use after the first stone went onto it. Enough of that, in enough fields, for long enough, and one of the heaps has a face in it.

There was never anyone in it, and the proof is public, and it is not a pleasant thing to watch. When one of these goes down the head goes first — it tips off the shoulders, lands, rolls a little — and for a moment there is a black socket where it was sitting. Everybody leans in the first time. The dark in it is about as deep as your hand and then it is stone: no cavity, no worn place shaped to fit anyone, nothing that was ever occupied. Then the body follows in a run of rubble, and what is on the ground is a heap again, moss and all, about the size it must have started at. It stays a heap for a good long while. It does not always stay one.

Among the fallen stones there is usually something harder than the rest. A split geode still leaking cold light. A six-sided point of white quartz. A teal crystal with a working edge on it. Now and then raw gold sitting in rubble-grade rock, which is the find people go up for. The ones who crack them for a living hold that a thing like this has to gather around something to begin with, and that it takes whatever in the ground is hardest and least arguable and grows outward from there. Gold is the one substance the dead of every century remember the same way. If you were assembling a body out of nothing but agreement, that is where you would start too. And past all of that, at the middle, there is one thing more: mossed plates shut around a small yellow-green star, warm to hold. Growth is not the soft half of anything. Watch a root take a wall apart and you know what green does to stone, given time; the star hands that over all at once, out of the edge of a blade, and then spends the rest of the fight closing you up while you are busy elsewhere.

Look at where the green is. The crown, the shoulder tops, the outsides of the arms, one flank — the faces that catch weather, and none of the faces that do not. Moss does not grow on a thing that moves. It grew there in the field, through season after season of holding one attitude, and it is the only part of the whole arrangement that was ever alive. Which is about right for what anybody keeps of a big old rock at the edge of a field. Not the rock. The rock was never in question. What stays with you is that it was green on one side, and that things were living on it.
